unit.title: Funds and ETFs
unit.description: Funds, ETFs, fees, index investing and how to read their factsheet

texts: Who does what?
An **investment fund** pools the money of thousands of people, who buy **units**, and invests it according to a policy. Who does each job?
Management company
Custodian
CNMV
Decides what the fund buys
The management company invests according to the fund's policy.
Holds the fund's assets
The custodian keeps safe whatever the fund buys.
Registers and supervises Spanish funds
The CNMV is Spain's markets regulator.
Checks the management company follows the rules
The custodian also keeps an eye on the management company.
Calculates the net asset value every day
The fund's assets divided by its units, once a day.
Warns about unauthorised firms
On its website you can check who's registered.
Sort all six jobs.
Each piece watches another, and the fund's money **belongs to the unitholders**, kept apart from the management company's: if the management company goes bust, it can't take it with it.
Hint: one decides, another holds and watches, and the CNMV supervises.
Sort each job
Switching funds
Pablo
I've got €5,000 in a fund, with €1,000 of gains.
I've found a similar one that's cheaper. How do I switch?
What do you tell him?
Sell, and use the money to buy the new one
Selling means paying tax on the €1,000 gain: about €190 to Hacienda (the Spanish tax office).
Ask for a transfer from the old fund to the new one
That's it! In Spain, a fund transfer isn't taxed. He'll pay when he sells out completely.
Wait until you don't have any gains
That could take years. With a transfer he switches today, without paying.
Careful: for it to count as a transfer, the money can't pass through your account.

steps.title: Active or index
steps.body:
There are **actively managed** funds (the manager picks investments to try to beat the index) and **index** funds (they copy an index at low cost).

The price of each unit, the **net asset value (NAV)**, is calculated once a day. And a fund doesn't guarantee gains: its value goes up and down with what it holds.
steps.key: A fund pools many people's money to buy many assets, with a management company in charge.
steps.tip: Transferring between funds is like changing lanes without paying a toll.

texts: ETF or traditional fund?
An **ETF** is a fund, almost always tracking an index, that **trades on the stock exchange** like a share. Is it an ETF thing or a traditional fund thing?
ETF
Traditional fund
You buy it at 11:37 at the price on your screen
An ETF trades all session long: its price changes from moment to moment.
You swap it for another without paying tax
Tax-free transfers are the fund's big advantage in Spain.
You pay the broker's commission and the spread
It's bought on the stock exchange, with the usual trading costs.
Its price is calculated once a day
A fund's net asset value is set once every day.
Every sale at a profit is taxed, even if you reinvest
In Spain, ETFs don't get the fund transfer rules.
You buy it through the management company, a bank or a platform
A traditional fund isn't listed: you subscribe to it directly.
Sort all six features.
An ETF is bought and sold **on the stock exchange, like a share**, and the big ones cost from **0.03 % to 0.30 %** a year. In Spain, the traditional fund has the advantage of **tax-free transfers**.
Hint: is it traded on the stock exchange or not?
Sort each feature
«Like a share»
Nora
Someone told me an ETF is «like a share».
So is it just as risky as buying a single company?
What do you tell her?
Yes, just as risky
You buy it like a share, but inside there are hundreds or thousands of companies.
You buy it like a share, but inside there's a basket of lots of companies
That's it! An MSCI World one holds more than a thousand companies from developed countries.
It has no risk at all
It has the index's risk: if the market falls 30 %, so does the ETF.
An index ETF is like buying the whole supermarket instead of a single product.

steps.title: UCITS ETFs
steps.body: A retail investor in the EU buys European **UCITS** ETFs, which come with a **KID**. Many US ETFs can't be sold to European retail investors because they don't have a KID.
steps.key: An ETF is a fund, almost always an index one, that you buy and sell on the stock exchange like a share.
steps.tip: Before buying an ETF, look for «UCITS» in its name and read its KID.

u10l3.title: Fees: the TER and hidden costs

texts: The cost you can't see
The same **€10,000** and the same market: 7 % a year before costs. One fund charges **0.2 %** a year; the other, whatever you choose.
Over 30 years, one fund charges 0.2 % and another 1.5 %. How much does the difference take?
Not much: about 1 % of the result
Almost a third of the result
More than half
The cost is charged **every year** and compounds: the cheap one ends at €71,968 and the expensive one at €49,840. That's **€22,128**, or 31 %.
Set the expensive fund to 1.5 % and see what happens over 30 years.
The **TER** (ongoing charges) never arrives as a bill: it's taken little by little out of the fund's value. Over 30 years, 1.5 % a year takes **almost a third** of your money.
Almost a third of your money, gone on fees!
Keep going: with more years, the gap shoots up.
Raise the expensive fund's fee and the years
The star team
Ana
Bank adviser
Ana, I recommend our equity fund. It's run by a star team.
And how much does it charge?
2 % a year. You're paying for quality.
A similar index fund charges 0.2 %.
What should Ana think?
If it's a star team, it's worth it
It would have to beat the index by 1.8 points a year, year after year. Hardly anyone manages that.
The expensive one has to earn 1.8 points more every year just to break even
That's it! The cost is guaranteed; beating the index isn't.
She should try it for a year and compare
One year tells you little: it could be luck. The cost, on the other hand, is always paid.

steps.title: Hidden costs
steps.body:
An index fund might charge 0.1-0.3 % a year; many active funds in Spain, 1.5 % or more. You'll see it in the **KID**, as ongoing charges.

On top of the TER: the broker's commission per trade, *spread*, custody fees, currency exchange and, for some funds, entry or exit fees. Add them all up.
steps.key: Every 1 % a year in costs eats a huge chunk of the result, because of compound interest.
steps.tip: 1.5 % a year sounds like nothing. Over 30 years, it's almost a third of your money.

texts: Be an active manager
Your job: guess where the market is heading. Four real indices: do they go up or down over the next few sessions?
Play all four rounds.
Getting it right sometimes is easy; getting it right **year after year** is almost impossible. According to SPIVA, over 10 years **97 %** of European equity funds lagged their index.
Four out of four! Could you do it again ten years in a row?
Getting it right sometimes is easy. Getting it right every time, almost impossible.
Up or down? Choose in each round
The +45 % fund
Bruno
I know which fund to buy: the top one in the rankings.
It went up 45 % last year! The manager's a genius.
What do you tell him?
Good idea: if it went up that much, it'll do it again
Very few repeat it. Often, the one that rises most is the one that took on the most risk.
Last year's rankings barely predict next year's: look at costs and policy
Nice! Chasing last year's winner usually ends badly.
Buy the top five, just in case
Five one-year winners aren't five ten-year winners.
Past returns say little about the future. Costs, on the other hand, keep coming back.

steps.title: Sharpe's arithmetic
steps.body:
1. All investors together **are** the market.
2. Before costs, the average active investor earns the same as the market.
3. After costs, they **must** earn less.

It's not that managers are bad: they compete against each other and charge more. SPIVA (Europe, end of 2025): over just **1 year**, **81.8 %** of European equity funds were already behind their index. Buffett won a 10-year bet with an S&P 500 index fund against a selection of *hedge funds*.
steps.key: Over the long run, the vast majority of active funds return less than their index, mainly because of costs.
steps.tip: If hardly anyone beats the index, buying the index already puts you ahead of almost everyone.

texts: Acc or Dist?
Two versions of the same fund, with the **same companies** inside: the only difference is what happens to the dividends. Which one does each feature belong to?
Accumulating (Acc)
Distributing (Dist)
Pays money into your account every quarter
The distributing one pays you the dividends, usually every quarter or every six months.
Reinvests the dividends inside the fund
You get nothing paid out: your units are worth more.
You pay tax on the dividends every year
What you receive is taxed that year, with 19 % withheld.
You pay no tax until you sell
The dividends keep compounding without passing through Hacienda (the Spanish tax office).
Useful for living off the income in retirement
If you need regular income, distributing fits.
For growing your money over 30 years
Reinvesting and deferring tax helps everything compound.
Sort all six features.
Accumulating **reinvests and defers tax**; distributing pays you income that's taxed every year. The ETF's name tells you: «Acc» or «Dist».
Hint: does it pay you the dividends or reinvest them?
Sort each feature
Seeing the money
Lucía
I prefer the distributing one: that way I «see» the money.
With the accumulating one it feels like I'm not earning anything.
Lucía has €10,000 in a fund that pays out 3 % in dividends.
What do you tell her?
You're right, the accumulating one gives you nothing
It does: her €300 get reinvested and her units are worth more.
You earn the same, just reinvested, and you pay tax later
That's it! With the distributing one she'd receive €300, but after withholding she'd get €243.
It doesn't matter, pick whichever you like
Before tax they return the same. If you don't need the income, accumulating usually wins.
Not seeing the money doesn't mean you're not earning it.

steps.title: Which suits each stage
steps.body:
To **build up** wealth over years, the accumulating version is usually more efficient: the €300 keep working. The distributing one makes sense if you **need income** (in retirement, for example).

It's not that one returns more: what changes is when you pay tax.
steps.key: Accumulating reinvests and defers tax; distributing pays you income that's taxed every year.
steps.tip: Look at the ETF's name: «Acc» or «Dist» tells you which it is.

texts: Physical or synthetic?
Two ways to copy an index: **buy** what's inside it, or have a bank **pay** you whatever it does. Which is which?
Physical replication
Synthetic replication
Buys the shares in the index
It holds the same as the index, at the same weights.
Signs a swap with a bank
The bank, the counterparty, pays it whatever the index does.
Buys only a representative sample
Sampling replication: useful for indices with thousands of stocks.
Holds a different basket of assets as collateral
Through the swap it gets the index's return in exchange for its basket's.
Lends out some of its shares for a fee
That's securities lending, backed by collateral.
Its exposure to the bank is capped at 10 %
The UCITS rules cap counterparty exposure at 10 % of the fund.
Sort all six features.
**Physical:** it buys what's in the index. **Synthetic:** a bank pays it what the index does, often very precisely; its own particular risk is that bank failing.
Hint: does it hold the shares or a contract with a bank?
Sort each feature
Two ETFs on the same index
Ana
I can't decide between two ETFs on the same index. One's physical, with a 0.07 % TER. The other's synthetic, at 0.05 %.
I'll just go for the cheaper one, right?
What else should she look at?
Nothing: always the cheapest
The TER matters, but so does how far it really strays from the index, and its size.
The actual tracking difference, the size and the replication method
Nice! Those are the pieces for comparing two ETFs on the same index.
How many years it's been on the market
It helps a bit, but the key is how far it strays and its size.
Two ETFs on the same index aren't identical: check how far each one strays.

steps.title: How far it strays
steps.body:
**Tracking difference** is how far the ETF falls behind (or gets ahead of) its index over a year. It's usually similar to the TER.

Synthetic replication can track the index very precisely and, in some cases, save on tax. Look at the tracking difference alongside the ETF's size and its replication method.
steps.key: Physical: it buys what's in the index. Synthetic: a bank pays it what the index does.
steps.tip: Neither kind of replication is bad: what matters is understanding the risk each one adds.

texts: Is it in the KID?
Every fund or ETF sold to retail investors in the EU has a **KID**: 3 pages at most, always with the same sections. What will you find?
It's in the KID
It isn't
The costs
Always: what you pay each year and all the other costs.
The risk indicator, from 1 to 7
From 1 (lowest risk) to 7 (highest).
The salesperson's opinion
The KID has a fixed, objective format: no opinions.
The recommended holding period
How long you should hold it.
A guaranteed return
Its performance scenarios are simulations, not promises.
What happens if the provider can't pay
It's one of the mandatory sections, like how to complain.
Sort all six items.
In 3 pages, the KID tells you **what you're buying, how much it can hurt and what it costs**. Its scenarios (stress, unfavourable, moderate, favourable) are simulations, not promises.
Hint: the KID is objective, with no opinions or guarantees.
Sort each item
«It's an opportunity»
Laura
Salesperson
Laura, this is an opportunity. You need to get in now.
The KID says: risk indicator 7. Recommended holding period: 1 day.
I don't quite get the product's objective…
What does Laura do?
She buys it: if it has a KID, it's safe
Having a KID only means it gives information, not that it's right for her.
She doesn't buy it until she understands what it is and how much she could lose
Nice! Risk 7 and a one-day horizon: a complex, speculative product.
She buys a little to try it out
Trying something you don't understand isn't learning: it's gambling.
That's what the KID is for: seeing in a minute that something isn't for you.

steps.title: What to look for in a minute
steps.body:
1. **ISIN:** the fund's ID card (12 characters; it starts with the country, like IE or LU).
2. **Objective and policy:** what does it buy?
3. **Risk indicator** (1-7): a money market fund is usually a 1; a global equity fund, around 4; a single-sector or emerging-markets fund, higher.
4. Annual **costs**.
5. **Recommended holding period.**
steps.key: In 3 pages, the KID tells you what you're buying, how much it can hurt and what it costs.
steps.tip: If you don't understand a product's KID, don't buy it.

u10l1-2.prompt: A fund has a net asset value of €12.50. You invest €1,000. How many units do you buy?

u10l1-3.prompt: A year later the net asset value is €13.75. How much are your 80 units worth?

u10l1-4.prompt: If the fund's management company goes bust, what happens to your money?
options: It's lost along with the management company
It's covered by the Fondo de Garantía de Depósitos (deposit guarantee scheme)
It still belongs to the unitholders: the fund's assets are kept separate
u10l1-4.explanation: The fund's assets don't belong to the management company. Careful: Spain's deposit guarantee scheme (FGD) covers deposits, not investment funds.

u10l1-6.prompt: In Spain you can move money from one fund to another without paying tax if you do it by transfer.
u10l1-6.explanation: You only pay when you finally cash out.

options: Usually charges more than 1 % a year
Changes the portfolio based on the manager's view
The manager picks companies to beat the index
u10l1-7.explanation: Active management tries to beat the index and charges more for it; index investing copies it cheaply.

u10l1-10.prompt: What advantages does a fund have over buying individual shares? Select all.
options: In Spain it can be transferred without paying tax
u10l1-10.explanation: A normal investment fund doesn't guarantee gains: its value goes up and down with what it holds.

u10l2-1.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
u10l2-1.explanation: These are the four words you'll see when you look up any ETF.
right: Basket of companies the ETF copies
Fund that trades on the stock exchange

u10l2-3.prompt: This chart is an index that several ETFs copy: an ETF tracking it will do the same, minus its costs. What did it do over the next 10 sessions?
u10l2-3.explanation: An index ETF doesn't remove the market's ups and downs: you get exactly what the index does, for better and for worse.

u10l2-4.prompt: What annual cost do the big index ETFs usually have?
u10l2-4.explanation: Copying an index is cheap: you don't need a team picking companies.

u10l2-6.prompt: Why can't a European retail investor buy many US ETFs?
options: Because investing in dollars is banned
Because they don't have a KID
u10l2-6.explanation: Without a KID, they can't be marketed to retail investors in the EU.

u10l2-7.prompt: You buy 15 units of an ETF at €98.40 and the broker charges a €2 commission. How much do you pay in total?

u10l2-10.prompt: The ETFs a retail investor can buy in the EU usually carry the ____ label.
u10l2-10.explanation: It's the European framework that sets rules on diversification, custody and disclosure.

u10l3-1.prompt: €10,000 over 30 years at 7 % a year with no costs grows to €76,123. With 1 % in annual costs (6 % net), how much? (round to the nearest euro)

u10l3-2.prompt: With those figures, how much does that 1 % a year cost you in total over 30 years? (round)
u10l3-2.explanation: 76,123 − 57,435 = €18,688: almost twice what you invested, just in costs.

u10l3-3.prompt: You have €20,000 in a fund with a TER of 1.8 %. How much do you pay this year?
u10l3-3.explanation: 20,000 × 1.8 % = €360. In an index fund at 0.2 % it would be €40.

u10l3-4.prompt: Where do you find a fund's ongoing charges?
options: On a monthly bill from the management company
u10l3-4.explanation: They're required to appear in the KID, along with the other costs.

u10l3-5.prompt: Which costs can reduce your return? Select all.
options: The fund having lots of unitholders
u10l3-5.explanation: So can the spread, custody fees and tax. The number of unitholders isn't a cost.

options: It's taken out of the fund's value every day, which is why you don't see it
Hacienda (the tax authority) collects it at the end of the year
u10l3-10.explanation: Not seeing a charge doesn't mean you're not paying: the TER has already been taken out of the net asset value.
feedback: That's it! It's the quietest cost: no bill arrives, but you pay it.
It isn't a tax: it's what the management company keeps.
It does: it comes out of the fund's value every day, which is why you don't see it.
lines: My fund charges 1.8 %, but nothing has ever been taken from my account 🤔

u10l4-1.prompt: According to SPIVA (Europe, end of 2025), what percentage of European equity funds lagged their index over 10 years?
u10l4-1.explanation: Over 1 year it was already 81.8 %; over 10 years, almost all of them.

u10l4-2.prompt: Out of 100 active European equity funds, how many beat their index over 10 years, going by that 97 %?
u10l4-2.explanation: 100 − 97 = 3. And the real problem is finding those 3 in advance.

u10l4-3.prompt: Put William Sharpe's reasoning in order.
options: Before costs, the average active investor earns the same as the market
The active investor pays more fees and trades more
After costs, the average active investor earns less
All investors together are the market
u10l4-3.explanation: It's pure arithmetic: it doesn't depend on whether managers are good or bad.

u10l4-7.prompt: According to Sharpe, why does the average active investor get less than the market?
options: Because managers don't know how to invest
Because before costs they earn the same, and then they pay more costs
u10l4-7.explanation: It's the arithmetic of active management (Sharpe, 1991).

u10l4-9.prompt: The report that compares active funds with their index is called ____.
u10l4-9.explanation: S&P Dow Jones Indices publishes it for Europe, the US and other regions.

u10l4-10.prompt: Which conclusions are reasonable from SPIVA? Select all.
options: Costs explain a large part of the gap
It's hard to know in advance who will beat the index
No active manager has ever beaten the market
Most active funds don't beat their index over the long run
u10l4-10.explanation: Some do beat it; the problem is that they're few and almost impossible to spot in advance.

u10l5-1.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
u10l5-1.explanation: Accumulating and distributing only change what's done with the dividends and when they're taxed.
right: Pays the dividends to the unitholder
You don't pay until you sell
The 19 % taken off when you're paid

u10l5-2.prompt: A distributing ETF pays you €400 in dividends this year. With 19 % withheld, how much reaches you?
u10l5-2.explanation: 400 × 0.81 = €324. The other €76 go to Hacienda this year.

u10l5-3.prompt: In Spain, which version is usually more tax-efficient for building wealth over years?
u10l5-3.explanation: Since it doesn't pay out, you're not taxed on the dividends until you sell, and everything keeps compounding.

u10l5-4.prompt: Marta, already retired, wants to top up her pension with income every quarter. Pablo, 24, wants his money to grow for 30 years. Which version suits each of them?
u10l5-4.explanation: The right version depends on whether you need income now or want to grow your wealth.
feedback: Pablo would pay tax every year on dividends he doesn't need.
Good: Marta needs income; Pablo needs his money to compound without paying tax every year.
The other way round: Marta would have to sell units to get income and Pablo would pay tax for no reason.

u10l5-7.prompt: You invest €10,000 in an accumulating fund that receives 3 % a year in dividends and reinvests them. Not counting price rises, how much would you have after 2 years? (round)

u10l5-10.prompt: What a distributing fund pays out is taxed in the year you ____ it.
u10l5-10.explanation: That's why, if you don't need that income, you pay tax earlier than you have to.

u10l6-1.prompt: What's true of a physically replicated ETF? Select all.
options: It may buy just a representative sample
It may lend out securities in exchange for a fee
It depends on a swap with a bank
It buys the shares in the index
u10l6-1.explanation: The swap belongs to synthetic replication.

u10l6-2.prompt: What are the features of synthetic replication? Select all.
options: Under UCITS, counterparty exposure is capped at 10 %
It doesn't track the index at all
u10l6-2.explanation: It tracks the index, often very precisely; its particular risk is the counterparty.

u10l6-3.prompt: In a synthetic ETF, who pays the index's return?
options: The swap counterparty, usually a bank
u10l6-3.explanation: The bank commits to paying whatever the index does in exchange for what the ETF's basket returns.

u10l6-5.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
u10l6-5.explanation: These are the pieces for understanding how an ETF copies its index and how precisely.
right: How far it strays from the index in a year
Buys every stock in the index

u10l6-6.prompt: An index rises 10.00 % in a year and the ETF that replicates it, 9.78 %. What is the tracking difference in points?
u10l6-6.explanation: 10.00 − 9.78 = 0.22 points, in line with what a cheap ETF costs.

u10l6-10.prompt: In a synthetic ETF, the bank it signs the swap with is called the ____.
u10l6-10.explanation: If the counterparty fails, the ETF can lose up to what it's owed, which UCITS caps at 10 %.

u10l7-1.prompt: Extract from a (fictional) KID: «Example World Fund, Acc class. ISIN IE00XXXXXXXX. Objective: to replicate the MSCI World index. Risk indicator: 4 out of 7. Ongoing charges: 0.20 % a year. Recommended holding period: 5 years». What level of risk does it indicate?
options: Medium: 4 on a scale of 1 to 7
u10l7-1.explanation: A 4 out of 7 is typical for a global equity fund: it swings quite a bit, but it's diversified.

u10l7-2.prompt: Extract from a (fictional) KID: «Example World Fund, Acc class. ISIN IE00XXXXXXXX. Objective: to replicate the MSCI World index. Risk indicator: 4 out of 7. Ongoing charges: 0.20 % a year. Recommended holding period: 5 years». If you invest €5,000, how much will you pay a year in ongoing charges?

u10l7-3.prompt: What will you always find in a KID? Select all.
options: The guaranteed return for the next 5 years
u10l7-3.explanation: The scenarios are simulations: a KID never guarantees returns.

u10l7-4.prompt: Match each item in the KID to what it tells you.
u10l7-4.explanation: With these four items you already know what it is, how much it can hurt, what it costs and what timeframe it's designed for.
right: How much it can swing, from 1 to 7
How long you should hold it
The code that identifies the fund

u10l7-5.prompt: Order from lowest to highest typical risk indicator.
u10l7-5.explanation: The more concentrated and volatile what it buys, the higher the indicator.

u10l7-7.prompt: The 12-character code that identifies a fund is called the ____.
u10l7-7.explanation: With the ISIN you can find the exact fund at any broker or on the CNMV website.
